paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The story of the series so far.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie found a magic tree house full of books. If they point to a picture in a book, they can go to that time and place. No time passes at home while they are away.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie eventually found out that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay,
paragraphs.simple: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from Camelot. Jack and Annie have done many missions for Morgan and Merlin. Teddy and Kathleen, two young enchanters, sometimes help them.

background.note: Camelot is King Arthur's castle and kingdom in old British stories.
Merlin is the most famous magician in the King Arthur stories.

paragraphs.context: The day was cloudy and windy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is reading a book about caring for a puppy and marking important parts with a yellow pen.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: Jack always studies everything carefully.

paragraphs.context: A scruffy black-and-white puppy raced after the ball and caught it in his mouth.
paragraphs.simple: Oki catches the ball but runs away instead of bringing it back.

background.note: Oki is the puppy Jack and Annie found at the end of Balto of the Blue Dawn (book 54).

paragraphs.context: “Yes, he does,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says Oki did fetch the ball. She takes the ball from him and asks Jack to go to the dog park.

paragraphs.context: “Yep.” Jack highlighted a paragraph about puppy dental care.
paragraphs.simple: Jack marks a part about a puppy's teeth, then puts the book and his pen in his backpack.

paragraphs.context: “Wait. Let’s see if he’ll walk with us on his own,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to see if Oki will walk with them without a leash. Jack thinks he will run away.

paragraphs.context: “I thought we could stop at the pet store,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack talks about buying a dog toothbrush. Before he finishes, Oki runs off down the street.

background.note: Vets say you should brush a dog's teeth with special dog toothpaste. People toothpaste can make dogs sick.

paragraphs.context: But the puppy kept running.
paragraphs.simple: Oki crosses the street, jumps over the curb and runs into the Frog Creek woods.

paragraphs.context: “Oki!” Annie shouted. She and Jack raced into the woods after the puppy.
paragraphs.simple: They run after Oki. It is autumn: branches move in the wind and dry leaves make noise.

background.note: In the Magic Tree House books, Frog Creek has all four seasons. Autumn (fall) in Pennsylvania is famous for colorful leaves.

paragraphs.context: “You were right!” wailed Annie. “We should have put him on the leash!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie cries that Jack was right; they should have used the leash. Jack says they will find him.

paragraphs.context: “Yes!” Annie and Jack took off running between the trees.
paragraphs.simple: They follow the barking and find Oki at the bottom of the big oak tree.

paragraphs.context: The magic tree house was nestled high in the treetop.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house sits high in the tree. Annie wonders how Oki knew it was there.

background.note: The magic tree house always has a rope ladder. Jack and Annie climb it at the start and end of every adventure.

paragraphs.context: “Teddy?” Jack called, looking up at the tree house. “Teddy?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack calls Teddy, but no one answers.

background.note: Teddy is a young enchanter who works in Morgan le Fay's library. He has helped Jack and Annie on several earlier Merlin Missions.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, you’re coming with us!” Annie said to Oki.
paragraphs.simple: Annie puts Oki in Jack's backpack. Jack carries him up the ladder.

paragraphs.context: When they had all climbed into the tree house, Jack took off his pack and set it on the floor.
paragraphs.simple: Oki sniffs every corner. There is no message from Merlin and no book from Morgan.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up and saw a scrap of paper floating on the wind.
paragraphs.simple: A piece of paper is flying in the wind. Annie runs down and catches it.

paragraphs.context: “See for yourself!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie climbs back up and gives Jack the note. She says it is about their favorite place.

paragraphs.context: Please come to Camelot.
paragraphs.simple: The note only asks them to come to Camelot.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, but it doesn’t look like Merlin or Morgan’s handwriting, or Teddy’s
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees that the writing is not Merlin's, Morgan's or Teddy's. He wonders who wrote it and why.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is the enchantress and librarian who owns the magic tree house. In the old legends she is King Arthur's half sister.

paragraphs.context: “Of course,” said Jack. They had visited the kingdom many times.
paragraphs.simple: Jack loves Camelot's fruit trees, the Great Hall, Morgan's library and their friends there. But he feels something is strange.

background.note: In a medieval castle, the Great Hall was the big main room where people ate, held parties and met the king.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry, Jack. Let’s just go,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie points at the word Camelot and wishes to go there.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was still.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house spins and then stops. Nothing moves.
paragraphs.tone: Every trip in the series starts with these same short lines.

paragraphs.context: Jack clutched Oki. He and the puppy both shivered in the damp, chilly air.
paragraphs.simple: Jack holds Oki. They shake in the cold, wet air.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, our clothes didn’t change,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Usually magic changes their clothes. This time it did not. Annie thinks the person who called them did not know how.

paragraphs.context: The tree house was in a forest of ancient-looking oak trees with gnarled roots and sprawling branches.
paragraphs.simple: The forest has very old oak trees with twisted roots. It is strangely quiet; there are no birds or squirrels.

background.note: Ancient oak forests once covered much of Britain. Oaks were sacred to the Druids, the priests of the old Celts.

paragraphs.context: “Let’s go down and get information firsthand,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: There is no book to help them, so Annie wants to go and see for themselves.

paragraphs.context: “So…which way?” Jack asked, looking around at the thick, towering oaks.
paragraphs.simple: The oaks are tall and thick. A few lines of sunlight come through the tops of the trees.

background.note: In thick forests, light comes through only small gaps in the leaves, so it falls in narrow beams, or shafts.

paragraphs.context: “Okay, but let’s put him on the leash this time,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Before Annie can put on the leash, Oki jumps out of her arms and runs away.

paragraphs.context: Racing through the woods, Jack and Annie chased Oki around one huge tree and then another.
paragraphs.simple: They chase Oki through light and shadow until he runs into a bright field of wheat.

background.note: In the Middle Ages, most people were farmers. Fields of wheat and other grain grew around castles.
Acorns are the nuts of oak trees. In the Middle Ages, farmers let their pigs eat acorns in the forest in autumn.

paragraphs.context: “You’ve got to stick with us, buddy,” said Jack as Annie attached the leash to the puppy’s collar.
paragraphs.simple: Annie catches Oki and puts on his leash.

paragraphs.context: With Oki pulling on his leash, Jack and Annie began pushing their way through the wheat.
paragraphs.simple: They push through the tall wheat. The sun shines on the tops of the stalks.

background.note: In medieval Britain, most people ate bread every day, so wheat and other grains were the most important crops.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, wow, look over there!” said Annie, pointing.
paragraphs.simple: They see red flags with dragons on tall towers. It is King Arthur's castle.

background.note: A red dragon is the symbol of Wales. In the old stories, King Arthur's father was Uther Pendragon ("Pendragon" means "chief dragon").

paragraphs.context: When they drew close, a trumpet sounded. A guard appeared between two turrets.
paragraphs.simple: As they come near the castle wall, a trumpet sounds and a guard appears.

paragraphs.context: The guard aimed a crossbow at them.
paragraphs.simple: The guard points a crossbow at them. Jack tells Annie to stop.

background.note: A crossbow shoots short, heavy arrows called bolts. It was a powerful weapon in the Middle Ages.

paragraphs.context: Oki barked wildly. Annie scooped him into her arms.
paragraphs.simple: Annie picks up Oki and tells the guard they come as friends.

paragraphs.context: “Jack! Annie!” someone called.
paragraphs.simple: A woman with golden hair and a green cape runs out. The guard puts down his weapon.

background.note: Queen Guinevere is King Arthur's wife in the old stories. Jack and Annie have met her before in Camelot.
In the Middle Ages, green cloth was often colored with plants, such as woad mixed with weld (a yellow dye).

paragraphs.context: “Hail, Your Majesty!” said Jack, bowing.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie greet the queen politely. Annie introduces Oki.

background.note: "Your Majesty" is the polite way to speak to a king or queen.

paragraphs.context: “Hello, Oki.” Though she smiled, Guinevere looked worried.
paragraphs.simple: The queen smiles but looks worried. Her hair is messy and her dress is torn.

background.note: Medieval queens wore long gowns of silk or wool, often with long sleeves and fur.

paragraphs.context: “Yes. Long ago, Morgan explained its magic to me,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan told the queen how to send the tree house for Jack and Annie if she ever needed help.

paragraphs.context: “I will explain everything,” said Guinevere.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says it is not safe outside the castle walls. She asks them to follow her.

paragraphs.context: Guinevere led them through the arched gateway.
paragraphs.simple: Inside the outer wall there are no knights, servants or workers.

paragraphs.context: “No, they left a fortnight ago,” said Guinevere.
paragraphs.simple: Merlin, Morgan, Teddy and Kathleen left two weeks ago. Only a few people are in Camelot.

background.note: This is a portcullis: a heavy iron or wooden gate that moves up and down to close a castle entrance.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie followed the queen across a wide courtyard.
paragraphs.simple: The stables and the forge are empty. Jack asks where everyone is.

background.note: In a castle, grooms took care of the horses: feeding, cleaning and saddling them.

paragraphs.context: “Ten days ago, enemy invaders came ashore in the distant east,
paragraphs.simple: Enemies came by sea. The king and his knights went to fight them. Some enemies came toward Camelot, so the queen took everyone to a hidden fort. Yesterday she came back with a few guards.

background.note: In the real history behind the Arthur stories, people from across the North Sea (Angles and Saxons) came to Britain by boat in the 400s and 500s.
Hill forts were old forts on hilltops with earth walls around them. Many can still be seen in Britain.

paragraphs.context: The queen sighed. Jack thought she looked as if she might cry.
paragraphs.simple: The queen almost cries, but she makes herself strong. At the fort she got terrible news.

paragraphs.context: “I will explain,” said the queen. “But first I must take you to a secret place.”
paragraphs.simple: In the Great Hall, tables are knocked over, plates are broken, old bread is on the floor, and the wall cloths are torn down.

background.note: The Great Hall was the biggest room in a medieval castle. People ate, met and sometimes slept there.

paragraphs.context: Jack remembered what the Great Hall had been like when he and Annie had attended a celebration there:
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers the hall as warm and bright with music. Now it is cold and broken.

background.note: Jack and Annie went to a Christmas celebration in the Great Hall in Magic Tree House #29, Christmas in Camelot.

paragraphs.context: “The invaders were looking for gold,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: The invaders took gold things from the chapel and the hall. The kitchen is empty and cold, and a rat runs across the floor.

background.note: Scullions were the lowest kitchen workers in a castle. They washed pots and did dirty jobs.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, no, Merlin and Morgan left with Teddy and Kathleen before word came of the invaders,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Merlin and Morgan do not know.
paragraphs.simple: Merlin and Morgan left before the news of the invaders came. The queen thinks they know nothing about it.

paragraphs.context: “I am afraid that is impossible,” the queen said.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says she cannot send them a message. She takes a torch and leads them down a narrow hall to a room.

paragraphs.context: Inhaling the sweet, woodsy smell of books, Jack recognized the room at once.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows the room at once by its smell. It is Morgan's library, full of books from all times and places.

background.note: In the Middle Ages, books were very rare and costly because they were copied by hand. A library of many books was a great treasure.

paragraphs.context: “Fortunately, the thieves were not interested in books,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The thieves did not take any books. Jack is glad, because books are more valuable to him than gold.

paragraphs.context: “I’ll explain in a moment,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The queen opens another door. Sweet, wet air comes in from a green garden with tall stone walls.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, wow…a secret garden,” whispered Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie lets Oki off the leash, and he runs into the green plants.

paragraphs.context: Guinevere led Jack and Annie through the doorway and into the walled garden.
paragraphs.simple: They walk on a stone path past many flowers: lilies, daffodils, periwinkles and roses.

background.note: The daffodil is the national flower of Wales. Daffodils bloom in early spring.

paragraphs.context: “From her plants, Morgan makes inks and paints for the books of our scribes,”
paragraphs.simple: Morgan makes ink and paint for books and colors for wool from her plants.

background.note: Before printing, every book was copied by hand. Scribes wrote with ink made from plants, soot or minerals.
Long ago, all cloth colors came from plants, animals or minerals. For example, woad gave blue, and madder root gave red.

paragraphs.context: Guinevere pointed to raised earth beds in the center of the garden.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan grows flowers and herbs to cure everyday sicknesses and injuries.

background.note: Medieval monks and wise women grew herbs in gardens to make medicine. Many modern medicines first came from plants.

paragraphs.context: “Nettles for a cold,” said Guinevere, “and mint for headaches.”
paragraphs.simple: The queen names plants used as medicine: nettles for colds, mint for headaches, lemongrass for fever and yarrow to stop bleeding.

background.note: Yarrow's Latin name, Achillea, comes from the Greek hero Achilles, who in legend used it to heal his soldiers' wounds.
Nettles sting if you touch them, but cooked nettles were eaten as a vegetable and used as medicine.

paragraphs.context: Jack shivered. The air felt tingly and alive.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels that someone is watching. He thinks he hears breathing, whispering or wings. Maybe it is only the wind.

paragraphs.context: Oki started barking. He bounced up and down, yelping at something in the shrubbery.
paragraphs.simple: Oki barks at something in the bushes. It is a small bronze dragon statue.

paragraphs.context: Annie started to pick up the puppy.
paragraphs.simple: Oki runs to the roses and finds a dragon made of pink stone.

background.note: Granite is a very hard stone. It can be gray, pink or black.

paragraphs.context: Oki kept bounding around the garden, yelping at more and more hidden dragon statues:
paragraphs.simple: Oki finds many hidden dragon statues made of clay, green stone, marble, silver, glass and seashells.

background.note: Emeralds are green gemstones. Some of the oldest known emerald mines were in ancient Egypt.

paragraphs.context: “No,” the queen said. “These dragons are far more than garden decorations.”
paragraphs.simple: The queen says the dragons are very important. She asks about Uther Pendragon, King Arthur's father.

background.note: In the old legends, Uther Pendragon was king of Britain and the father of Arthur. Merlin helped him.

paragraphs.context: The queen nodded. “Indeed, it does,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: A dragon was on Uther's flag and shield, and now it is on Arthur's. The dragon is the sign of the ruler of Camelot.

background.note: Knights and kings had pictures on their shields and flags so people could tell who they were in battle. This is called heraldry.

paragraphs.context: “Before he died, Uther Pendragon ordered his craftsmen to create nine dragon statues.
paragraphs.simple: Uther had nine dragon statues made, each from a different material.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said the queen. “Merlin placed a spell on each of them.
paragraphs.simple: Merlin put a spell on the dragons. While they are in the garden, enchanters can open magic doors to nine magic lands.

paragraphs.context: “They are lands that cannot be traveled to directly from mortal worlds,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: Ordinary people cannot go to these lands. Jack and Annie have been to four of them with Merlin's help.

background.note: In Magic Tree House #29, Christmas in Camelot, Jack and Annie go to the Otherworld to find the Water of Memory and Imagination.

paragraphs.context: “And the marble dragon opens the portal to the Land-Behind-the-Clouds,” said Guinevere.
paragraphs.simple: The marble dragon opens the way to the Land-Behind-the-Clouds, where they met the Ice Wizard.

background.note: Jack and Annie went to the Land-Behind-the-Clouds and met the Ice Wizard in Magic Tree House #32, Winter of the Ice Wizard.

paragraphs.context: “The bronze dragon is the gateway to the realm of the Raven King,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The bronze dragon opens the way to the Raven King's land, and the seashell dragon to the Sea Serpent's land.

background.note: Haunted Castle on Hallows Eve (#30) has the Raven King.
In Summer of the Sea Serpent (#31), Jack and Annie become seals and meet Kathleen, a selkie (a seal girl).

paragraphs.context: “There are five realms you have not visited,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The most important dragon is the gold one. It opens the way to Avalon. Merlin, Morgan, Teddy and Kathleen went there two weeks ago to rest.

background.note: In the King Arthur legends, Avalon is a magic island. After his last battle, Arthur is taken there to heal.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, but in this case, a vacation with a bit of magic,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan and Merlin rest in Avalon. It has a huge garden with old secrets of healing; only there can Morgan grow plants that heal all wounds.

paragraphs.context: The ninth statue—the gold dragon—occupies the most important place in the garden,
paragraphs.simple: The gold dragon should be among the yellow roses in the corner of the garden.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie hurried over to the rosebushes. But there was no dragon.
paragraphs.simple: There is no dragon in the roses. The queen says it has been stolen.

paragraphs.context: “When the invaders plundered the castle, they found their way into this garden,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The invaders stole the gold dragon because they wanted gold. Without it, the door to Avalon is closed, and their friends cannot come back.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said Guinevere. “Avalon is where they are, and Avalon is where they will remain
paragraphs.simple: Their friends will stay in Avalon unless the dragon is found. Annie says they must find it.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said the queen. “And there is another reason to find the gold statue.
paragraphs.simple: A messenger told the queen that King Arthur has a wound that will kill him.

paragraphs.context: Guinevere took a deep breath.
paragraphs.simple: An arrow went through Arthur's armor into his chest near his heart. He must go to Avalon soon, or he will die.

background.note: Knights wore chain mail (small metal rings linked together) or metal plates. Arrows from strong bows could still go through it.

paragraphs.context: “Yes. Right now we have a small supply of healing water from Avalon that is keeping Arthur alive,”
paragraphs.simple: A little healing water from Avalon keeps Arthur alive, but it will not last long.

paragraphs.context: “Your courage and intelligence are legendary in Camelot,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says Jack and Annie are famous for being brave and clever. She asks them to help find the gold dragon.

paragraphs.context: “Yes. Sir Tristan and Sir Lamorak brought him back to Camelot two nights ago,”
paragraphs.simple: Two knights, Sir Tristan and Sir Lamorak, brought the king home.

background.note: Sir Tristan is a Knight of the Round Table, famous for the love story of Tristan and Isolde.
Sir Lamorak was one of the strongest Knights of the Round Table in Thomas Malory's book Le Morte d'Arthur.

paragraphs.context: Oki scampered ahead with the queen as she led the way back through the library
paragraphs.simple: They go back through the library and the courtyard to a small chapel.

background.note: Cobblestones are round stones set into the ground to make a road. Many old European towns still have cobbled streets.

paragraphs.context: A bearded knight stared at Jack and Annie with dark, tired eyes.
paragraphs.simple: Two tired knights guard the chapel. Oki growls at them.

background.note: Knights used long lances on horseback in battles and in jousting, a sport where two knights ride at each other.

paragraphs.context: Without a word, the two knights bowed to the queen, then strode across the courtyard.
paragraphs.simple: The knights bow and walk away. The queen asks Jack and Annie into the chapel.

paragraphs.context: “Thank you for coming, my friends,” a man said in a low, hoarse voice.
paragraphs.simple: King Arthur sits in a wooden chair under a colored glass window. His face is very pale.

background.note: Stained-glass windows have pieces of colored glass that make pictures. They were common in medieval churches.
Before electric light, churches and castles used candles and oil lamps. Good candles were made of beeswax and were expensive.

paragraphs.context: “Oki, stay!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Oki jumps into the king's lap and licks his face. The king smiles, but his eyes show pain.

paragraphs.context: “No talk…of that,” the king said, struggling to breathe.
paragraphs.simple: The king can hardly breathe, but he says he will win.
paragraphs.tone: The dots (…) show that he speaks slowly and with pain.

paragraphs.context: “No…I must explain,” said the king.
paragraphs.simple: Deep in the forest lives Cafelle, an old woman who can see the future. She was Arthur's nursemaid. She can help find the dragon.

background.note: Seers in old stories could see the future. In the Arthur legends, Merlin is also a seer.
In rich medieval families, a nursemaid looked after the children. In the legends, Arthur was raised away from his parents, by Sir Ector.

paragraphs.context: “Yes…yes…,” the king said. “The tree leaves speak to her…in the wind.
paragraphs.simple: The king says the leaves speak to Cafelle in the wind. Jack worries the king is confused.

paragraphs.context: Guinevere placed a hand on her husband’s shoulder.
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle listens to the trees in a trance. Then she tells her prophecies as riddles.

paragraphs.context: “We know that you are particularly brilliant at solving riddles,” said Guinevere.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie are good at solving riddles. If they solve Cafelle's riddle, they can find the dragon.

background.note: Jack and Annie have solved riddles on many earlier Merlin Missions.

paragraphs.context: “Good,” said the queen. “Sir Tristan and Sir Lamorak are preparing for our departure.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack is happy the knights will come. He hopes they will have a better plan.

paragraphs.context: “No, not you, my lord,” Queen Guinevere said.
paragraphs.simple: The queen wants the king to rest, but he says Cafelle will only tell her prophecies to him.

paragraphs.context: The queen took a deep breath. “Then so be it,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: The queen agrees. Jack and Annie help the king stand up.

paragraphs.context: A rumbling sound came from the stables.
paragraphs.simple: The knights drive a wooden hay cart pulled by two oxen across the courtyard.

background.note: Oxen are strong and slow. In the Middle Ages they pulled carts and plows more often than horses did.

paragraphs.context: “This is our carriage,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: Nobody will think the king is in a hay cart. Jack wonders how six people can fit.

paragraphs.context: The oxen came to a halt, and the knights climbed down from the drivers’ bench.
paragraphs.simple: The oxen stop. Sir Lamorak gives old cloaks to the king and queen as disguises.

paragraphs.context: The queen helped the king pull on his disguise,
paragraphs.simple: The queen helps the king put on his cloak. She changes her green velvet cape for an old gray cloak and hides her golden hair.

background.note: Velvet is a soft, thick cloth. In the Middle Ages it was very expensive and worn mostly by kings, queens and nobles.

paragraphs.context: Sir Tristan handed Jack and Annie two more ragged cloaks.
paragraphs.simple: Sir Tristan gives Jack and Annie old cloaks too, and they put them on.

paragraphs.context: Oki barked and squirmed in Annie’s arms as if he was eager to ride in the hay cart, too.
paragraphs.simple: The queen asks if Oki will ride in the back. Jack is surprised that he and Annie must drive.

paragraphs.context: King Arthur was lying in the hay with his eyes closed.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks Oki to take care of the king. Oki lies close to him.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie climbed up to the drivers’ bench.
paragraphs.simple: Annie takes the reins. Jack thinks the knights will ride horses next to the cart.

paragraphs.context: “Hike!” Annie shouted, using a command they’d learned from Alaskan dogsledders.
paragraphs.simple: Annie uses "Hike!", the word that tells sled dogs to start running.

background.note: Jack and Annie learned dog-sled commands in Alaska in Balto of the Blue Dawn (Magic Tree House #54).

paragraphs.context: “No, Jack. We will be traveling alone,” said Guinevere.
paragraphs.simple: They will travel alone, looking like a poor farm family, so enemies will not know them.

paragraphs.context: The oxen took a few steps forward.
paragraphs.simple: The oxen are joined by a wooden bar to a pole on the cart. They walk slowly over the stones.

paragraphs.context: As the oxen headed across the outer courtyard, Annie waved to the two knights,
paragraphs.simple: Annie waves to the knights, who quietly watch them go.

paragraphs.context: “Here we go,” Jack repeated softly. “Just us.”
paragraphs.simple: The cart rolls noisily out of the castle gate. Jack feels nervous because they are alone.

paragraphs.context: “Westward, toward the mountains,” said Queen Guinevere.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says to go west ("westward"), toward the mountains. Cafelle lives where the forest meets the heath.

background.note: Britain has many heaths and moors: wide, open, wild lands with heather and low bushes and few trees.

paragraphs.context: “Got it,” said Annie. “Haw!” she called to the oxen,
paragraphs.simple: Annie uses another dog-sled word: "Haw!" means "Turn left!"

background.note: Mushers say "Gee!" for right and "Haw!" for left. Farmers used the same words for oxen and horses long before dogsleds.

paragraphs.context: The heavy animals moved slowly toward the distant cloud-covered mountains.
paragraphs.simple: The oxen move slowly toward the mountains. A cool, wet wind blows through the grass by the road.

paragraphs.context: “We hope that our army is defeating them in the east,” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The army may be winning in the east, but small groups of invaders may still be moving around like wolves.

paragraphs.context: The hills and fields were covered with shadows of clouds scudding across the sun.
paragraphs.simple: Cloud shadows move over empty houses and burned trees and fields.

paragraphs.context: “No, the fires were set by those who live here,” answered the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The farmers burned their own crops and wood before they ran away, so the invaders could not have them.

background.note: Flax was grown all over medieval Europe. Its stems were made into linen cloth, and its seeds into linseed oil.
Barley was used to make bread, porridge and ale. It grows well in cold, wet places like Britain.

paragraphs.context: “When they know their king has returned,” the queen said.
paragraphs.simple: The people will only come back when they know the king is home. Jack sees that everything now depends on them.

paragraphs.context: As the oxen pulled the cart toward the wooded hills and plains at the base of the mountains,
paragraphs.simple: Near the mountains the air gets colder and the wind stronger. The road turns into a path full of weeds and thorny plants.

background.note: The thistle is the national flower of Scotland. A legend says a Viking stepped on one and cried out, which warned the Scots.

paragraphs.context: The oxen stopped moving, and the cart jolted to a halt.
paragraphs.simple: The cart stops suddenly. The queen wakes the king and says they must walk a short way.

paragraphs.context: “First, drink this,” said the queen, lifting the flask to the king’s lips.
paragraphs.simple: The king drinks healing water. Jack worries that there will not be enough for the whole trip.

paragraphs.context: Annie climbed down from the cart bench and grabbed Oki.
paragraphs.simple: The queen helps the king out of the cart, and they walk slowly down a path.

paragraphs.context: As Jack and Annie followed the royal couple through the shifting shadows of the forest,
paragraphs.simple: They cross a small old bridge and come to an open place with a little stone house and a stick fence. Smoke comes from the chimney.

background.note: Fences of woven sticks are called wattle fences. People in Britain made them for thousands of years.
Poor country people in old Britain often lived in one-room huts of stone or wood with a fire in the middle.

paragraphs.context: A moment later, an old woman wrapped in a shawl stood in the doorway.
paragraphs.simple: An old woman with a long white braid opens the door. Her eyes are closed, and Jack understands she is blind. A white dog with light blue eyes stands next to her.

background.note: Many white dogs with blue eyes are born deaf. Kee cannot hear.
Braiding long hair kept it neat and out of the way. People have braided hair for thousands of years.

paragraphs.context: Oki didn’t bark or whine. The peaceful gaze of the white dog seemed to keep him calm.
paragraphs.simple: The white dog's peaceful look keeps Oki calm.

paragraphs.context: Cafelle bowed her head. “Welcome, Your Majesty,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle cannot see, but she knows the queen and two children have come too.

paragraphs.context: “Annie.” The seer reached out, and Annie took her hand.
paragraphs.simple: Holding Annie's hand, Cafelle describes her: she loves animals, says what she thinks, and is brave. But she moves too fast and is not patient.

paragraphs.context: “You are very thoughtful and intelligent, Jack,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks carefully and loves books. But he worries too much and is too slow to act.

paragraphs.context: “Oki, you are a very happy and lively dog! Very curious and willful,” the seer said with a smile.
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle says Oki is happy and curious and likes his own way. Her dog Kee is old. Kee cannot hear and Cafelle cannot see, so they help each other.

paragraphs.context: Cafelle then held both her hands out to King Arthur, and he took them in his.
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle takes the king's hands and knows that he is wounded.

paragraphs.context: Inside, Jack could barely see anything. There were no windows and no lanterns.
paragraphs.simple: The hut is dark, with only a fire and two candles. Cafelle moves easily with Kee and makes the fire bigger.

background.note: In old houses the hearth was the center of the home. People cooked, kept warm and got light from it.
To start a fire without matches, people used flint and steel to make sparks, then lit dry kindling.

paragraphs.context: “Tell me, what do you seek to know, my lord?” Cafelle asked King Arthur.
paragraphs.simple: The king tells Cafelle the gold dragon was stolen. She understands he needs it to go to Avalon.

paragraphs.context: Cafelle nodded. Without another word, she stood up and opened the door.
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle and Kee stand in the doorway and face the woods.

paragraphs.context: Jack reached under his cloak and took off his backpack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack gets his pencil and notebook to write down the prophecy.

background.note: Jack always carries a notebook to write facts and clues. He has done this since the first Magic Tree House book.

paragraphs.context: For a long moment, all was quiet except for the gentle rustling of the trees.
paragraphs.simple: The sound of the leaves and wind gets louder and louder, as if the forest is shouting secrets. Then it becomes quiet again.

paragraphs.context: Cafelle turned to face the king. She began to speak in a clear voice:
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle says the riddle. Every line ends with the same sound (bright, night, white, sight, flight, light, fight).

background.note: Riddles and prophecies in old stories are often in rhyme, which made them easier to remember before people could read and write.

paragraphs.context: Jack wrote down her words as fast as he could.
paragraphs.simple: Jack writes quickly. Cafelle and Kee stand still in the doorway again.

paragraphs.context: The seer turned to him. “What did I say?” she whispered.
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle does not remember what she said. She seems half asleep. Jack reads it to her.

paragraphs.context: “Oh…I see…,” said Cafelle. She looked troubled.
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle looks worried. Jack is worried about the last two lines too.

paragraphs.context: “Munith Mor is the highest mountain in the west,” said Guinevere.
paragraphs.simple: Munith Mor is the highest mountain in the west. Cafelle tells them to keep going over the wild lands.

background.note: Munith Mor is not a real place. "Mor" means "big" in Scottish Gaelic and Irish (Gaelic "mòr").

paragraphs.context: “Good,” said Guinevere. “Jack and Annie, you will decipher the rest of the riddle as we travel.”
paragraphs.simple: They must go to Munith Mor, find the dragon and take it back to the garden.

paragraphs.context: “Ah,” the queen said. “That seems to say we will lose the fight if we do not arrive in Avalon before dawn.”
paragraphs.simple: They must do everything by tomorrow morning: go to the mountain, find the dragon and bring it back.

paragraphs.context: “My lady, you are trembling,” Cafelle said.
paragraphs.simple: The queen's voice shakes, but she stands tall. Jack wonders if she is afraid there is not enough time.

paragraphs.context: Jack put away his notebook and picked up his backpack.
paragraphs.simple: They go out into the cool, windy air. Oki barks at leaves blowing in the wind.

paragraphs.context: Jack glanced back at Cafelle and Kee standing in the doorway of the hut.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks Cafelle and Kee can hear and see more than other people because they help each other.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie hurried back to her. The seer reached into the pocket of her dress.
paragraphs.simple: Cafelle gives each of them a small red stone.

paragraphs.context: “Rocks from the mountains of fire before time,” said the blind woman.
paragraphs.simple: The stones come from very old volcanoes. Cafelle says to use them to save the king, with hope, courage and imagination.

background.note: Long ago, Scotland and northern England had many volcanoes. Edinburgh Castle stands on the rock of an old volcano.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t understand. “But what do we do with—”
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to know more, but the queen calls them, and Annie pulls him away.

paragraphs.context: “But I don’t understand,” Jack said to Annie. “What do we do with these stones?”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they will use their imaginations and work it out later. She runs off.

paragraphs.context: “Darn,” said Jack, annoyed. He crammed his stone into a pocket of his jeans and ran after the others.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is not happy. He pushes the stone into his pocket and runs after them.

paragraphs.context: Jack caught up with everyone at the footbridge.
paragraphs.simple: The king drinks more healing water. Jack worries again that it will run out.

paragraphs.context: “We must hurry,” Guinevere said quietly to Jack and Annie, “or all will be lost.”
paragraphs.simple: The queen says they must hurry. Annie asks Oki to keep the king warm.

paragraphs.context: In the failing light, the yoked oxen began lumbering up the road toward the distant mountain peaks.
paragraphs.simple: It is getting dark. The oxen walk slowly. Jack wonders how they can do everything before dawn.

paragraphs.context: “We need more information,” he said to Annie. “We should have learned more about the stones.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie argue, using Cafelle's words about each other: Annie is not patient, and Jack worries too much.

paragraphs.context: “No! Let’s discuss each line,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to look at the riddle one line at a time. Annie wants to think about the whole riddle.

paragraphs.context: In the distance, three horsemen in black cloaks were riding across a burnt field,
paragraphs.simple: Three riders in black come toward the road. The queen covers the king's face and hides her golden hair.

background.note: Long cloaks kept travelers warm and dry. Dark colors also made riders harder to see.

paragraphs.context: “Tell them your sister and your parents have a disease,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Jack to say that the family is sick. Oki barks so loudly that Jack can hardly hear her.

paragraphs.context: “I have a terrible disease, Jack,” Annie said. “Here, take the reins.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie gives Jack the reins and looks for something in his backpack, keeping her head down.

paragraphs.context: Oki barked louder as the riders galloped closer and closer.
paragraphs.simple: The men stop in front of the cart. They have dirty faces, rough beards and long, messy hair.

paragraphs.context: Jack pulled on the reins to stop the oxen. Oki barked and growled from the cart.
paragraphs.simple: Jack holds the reins so hard that his knuckles turn white.

paragraphs.context: The huge rider glared at him with small, mean eyes. “Who are you?” he snarled.
paragraphs.simple: The big rider looks at Jack angrily and asks who they are. Jack tries to keep his voice calm.

paragraphs.context: Annie didn’t look up. She was still hunched over the backpack.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is still bent over the backpack. Jack does not know what she is doing.

paragraphs.context: The rider glanced toward the back of the cart. “Who lies there?” he asked.
paragraphs.simple: The rider asks who is lying in the cart. "Who lies there?" is an old way of saying "Who is lying there?"

paragraphs.context: “Um…our mother and father…they’re sick,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says their parents and sister are sick. He has to shout because Oki is barking.

paragraphs.context: “Yellow fever!” Annie shouted. She threw off her hood and looked up at the men.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not know what to say. Annie throws off her hood and shouts "Yellow fever!"

background.note: Yellow fever is a real disease spread by mosquitoes. It can turn the skin yellow. It was not known in medieval Britain; it came from Africa and later spread to the Americas.

paragraphs.context: Jack nearly fell off the cart. Annie looked terrible!
paragraphs.simple: Annie's face is covered with bright yellow spots!

paragraphs.context: The men pulled back. Grunting and growling, they spurred their horses past the cart.
paragraphs.simple: The men are afraid of the disease, and they ride away fast.

background.note: Spurs are small metal points on a rider's boots. Riders press them into a horse's sides to make it go faster.

paragraphs.context: Annie held up the yellow marker from Jack’s backpack,
paragraphs.simple: Annie used Jack's yellow marker, the one he used in the puppy book, to make the spots.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked back at the king and queen. Arthur had slept through the whole incident.
paragraphs.simple: The king slept the whole time. The queen sits up, holding Oki, who is still barking.

paragraphs.context: “Annie saved us, Your Majesty,” said Jack. “She tricked them.
paragraphs.simple: When Annie turns around, the queen is scared by the spots. Then she understands and laughs.

paragraphs.context: “All right! Let’s get this show back on the road!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels happier after their success. He tells the oxen to go.
hardWords: get this show back on the road

paragraphs.context: The oxen started forward, and the queen settled back in the cart.
paragraphs.simple: Jack gives Annie his notebook and asks her to read the riddle again.

paragraphs.context: “Curtain of white,” Jack broke in.
paragraphs.mainIdea: What is a curtain of white?
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie think it may be a white curtain in a house or in front of a closet.

paragraphs.context: “Wait,” said Jack. “Does that mean the curtain hides from sight?
paragraphs.simple: Maybe the curtain is hiding something. They decide the robbers hid the gold dragon behind a white curtain.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Jack. “What if we run into them when we find the place with the curtain?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack worries about meeting the robbers. The yellow marker trick will not work in the dark.

paragraphs.context: Dark clouds covered the sky as the cart creaked and rattled over the weedy path.
paragraphs.simple: It looks like rain. The king is shaking, and the queen wipes his forehead.

background.note: The west of Britain gets a lot of rain because wet winds blow in from the Atlantic Ocean.

paragraphs.context: The queen looked up and caught Jack’s gaze. “He is very weak now,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: The queen says the king and his knights never give up, even without food or rest and in bad weather.

background.note: King Arthur's knights met at the Round Table. A round table has no head, so all knights were equal there.

paragraphs.context: “We do that, too,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie say they never give up either. Jack sits up straighter with pride.

paragraphs.context: The oxen pulled the cart past deserted farms, thatched huts, and clusters of orchards.
paragraphs.simple: There are fewer and fewer trees. At sunset they reach open land at the bottom of a mountain. There is no road.

background.note: Thatched roofs are made of dry straw or reeds. Many old cottages in Britain still have them.

paragraphs.context: The oxen started across the moorlands.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looks for houses or lights but sees none. He wonders where they will find a white curtain.

background.note: Moorlands are high, open lands with heather, grass and few trees. They often have peat (soft, wet, dark soil) underneath.

paragraphs.context: As the sky darkened to dusk, the wind blew harder and a thin drizzle started to fall.
paragraphs.simple: It starts to rain. Jack and Annie give their cloaks to the king and queen.

paragraphs.context: “No problem,” said Jack, though he was freezing.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it is no problem, but he is very cold. The light rain has become windy rain.

paragraphs.context: “I have never been there, Annie,” said Guinevere. “But Arthur has.
paragraphs.simple: Avalon is a big island in a hidden lake with mountains around it. It has green fields and apple trees.

paragraphs.context: “In truth, Avalon means ‘apples,’ ” said the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The name Avalon means "apples". The island has trees, flowers, birds, butterflies, and magic and real animals.

background.note: An old Welsh name for Avalon is Ynys Afallon, which means "Island of Apples". Some people say Avalon was at Glastonbury in England.

paragraphs.context: Oki barked. “Yes, like you,” the queen said, smiling at the puppy.
paragraphs.simple: In Avalon, swans pull boats and mermaids swim in the lake.

background.note: In some old stories, swans pull magic boats. In the German legend of Lohengrin, a knight arrives in a boat pulled by a swan.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, and Avalon has sunshine and gentle breezes and clear, starry nights all year long,
paragraphs.simple: As the queen talks about Avalon, the rain stops, the wind gets weaker and the air gets warmer. An almost full moon rises.

paragraphs.context: “Our most beautiful dreams and happiest thoughts come from Avalon,” said Guinevere.
paragraphs.simple: In Avalon there are songs, poems, plays, dancing and games.

paragraphs.context: The queen’s story was interrupted by a sudden jolt.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the cart jumps forward, and Jack and Annie fall off the bench onto the wet grass.

paragraphs.context: “Jack! Annie!” Guinevere cried. As she climbed out of the back of the cart,
paragraphs.simple: The queen climbs out to help. The king keeps sleeping.

paragraphs.context: “I see,” said the queen. The wooden pole that had been lashed to the oxen’s yoke had fallen to the ground.
paragraphs.simple: The old rope broke, so the oxen are not joined to the cart any more.

paragraphs.context: “No, I fear not,” the queen said, holding the pieces of the rope.
paragraphs.simple: The queen thinks they cannot get back to Camelot by morning now.

paragraphs.context: Finally Jack broke the silence. “We never give up,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers the queen's words: they never give up. He says they will walk.

paragraphs.context: “Then we’ll pull him in the cart,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says he and Annie can pull the cart themselves. The queen says she will pull too.

paragraphs.context: “Should we take the yoke off the oxen first?” Annie asked.
paragraphs.simple: They take the heavy wooden yoke off the oxen so the animals can go home alone.

background.note: A yoke is a wooden bar across the necks of two animals so they pull together. Oxen have worked in yokes for thousands of years.

paragraphs.context: “Go back home to Camelot,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: At first the oxen do not move. Then they walk slowly back across the moor.

paragraphs.context: “Come on, let’s get going,” said Jack. He picked up his pack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts his pack in the cart. Oki is lying on the sleeping king's chest.

paragraphs.context: All of them wrapped their arms around the wooden pole.
paragraphs.simple: The three of them lift the heavy pole, breathing hard.

background.note: People shout "Heave!" or "Heave-ho!" so that everyone pulls at the same moment. Sailors used it when pulling ropes.

paragraphs.context: “Onward!” said Jack. Gripping the pole, they struggled together,
paragraphs.simple: They try to pull, but the cart does not move at all.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, I’ll push,” said Jack. He went to the back of the cart and pushed.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushes so hard that he slips and falls, but he gets up and tries again.

paragraphs.context: As Jack pushed, Annie and Guinevere pulled from the front.
paragraphs.simple: At last the wheels turn, and the cart starts rolling.

paragraphs.context: Keep going echoed in Jack’s mind as he pushed the cart across the moor.
paragraphs.simple: Jack keeps hearing the words "keep going" in his mind. Even the wheels seem to say it.

paragraphs.context: Jack kept pushing while Annie and Guinevere kept pulling,
paragraphs.simple: Finally they arrive at the bottom of the mountain.

paragraphs.context: Then they all looked up at Munith Mor looming overhead.
paragraphs.simple: They look up at the big mountain above them.

background.note: The tallest mountain in Britain is Ben Nevis in Scotland, 1,345 meters high.

paragraphs.context: A stream of moonlit water splashed over the ridges of the mountainside.
paragraphs.simple: A white waterfall shines in the moonlight and falls into a pool. Everything is quiet except the water.

background.note: Britain's highest single-drop waterfall is Eas a' Chual Aluinn in Scotland, about 200 meters high.

paragraphs.context: “Are we in Avalon?” a deep voice rasped. King Arthur was sitting up in the hay.
paragraphs.simple: The king wakes up and asks if they are in Avalon. The queen says they are close.

paragraphs.context: As Guinevere helped Arthur from the back of the cart, Annie put Oki on the ground.
paragraphs.simple: It is too dark to read the notebook, so Jack and Annie say the riddle from memory.

paragraphs.context: “The moon is bright, and we’re at Munith Mor,” said Annie. “So where’s the curtain?”
paragraphs.simple: They look around at the empty land. There is no curtain.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, look at that waterfall!” said Annie. “Doesn’t it kind of look like a curtain?”
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees that the white waterfall looks like a curtain. Jack agrees.

paragraphs.context: “Hides from sight!” said Annie. “The waterfall’s hiding something!”
paragraphs.simple: They solve the riddle: the gold dragon is hidden behind the waterfall.

paragraphs.context: “We’re going to check it out. You guys stay here,” Annie said to the queen.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells the queen and king to stay. Then she uses a polite word for them: "Your Majesties".

background.note: "Your Majesty" is how you speak to one king or queen. For two, you say "Your Majesties".

paragraphs.context: “No! Go back!” Jack commanded.
paragraphs.simple: Oki will not go back, so Annie puts him in Jack's backpack.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, I need to wash off the yellow marks!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie washes the yellow marker spots off her face in the stream.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie climbed up to a rocky ledge and gazed at the cascade.
paragraphs.simple: From a rock shelf, Jack sees a rock sticking out. The water shoots over it, and there seems to be an opening behind the waterfall.

background.note: Some real waterfalls have caves behind them where people can walk, such as Seljalandsfoss in Iceland.

paragraphs.context: Jack followed Annie over the wet rocks to the waterfall.
paragraphs.simple: In the moonlight, Jack can just see an empty space in the rock behind the waterfall. It is a cave.

paragraphs.context: Yip! Yip! Oki popped his head out of Jack’s backpack.
paragraphs.simple: Oki barks as they go behind the waterfall into the cave.

paragraphs.context: The air in the cramped cave smelled of wet rocks and mold.
paragraphs.simple: The cave is small and smells wet. Jack has to bend down. Oki falls out of the backpack and runs away.

paragraphs.context: Oki’s barking came from deep within the cave.
paragraphs.simple: They feel the wall to find their way. The cave becomes a low tunnel, and they must crawl on hands and knees in the dark.

background.note: Many caves in Britain are in limestone rock, where water slowly dissolves the stone over thousands of years.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly Jack heard a flapping and squeaking off to the side.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears wings and squeaks: bats. Annie worries about spiders too.

background.note: Bats sleep in caves in the day and fly out at night. Most British bats eat insects. They find their way in the dark by listening to echoes.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt around blindly for the puppy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack touches something cold and smooth. He pulls his hand back, afraid it is a snake.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, there’s something else here,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie finds something like a heavy plate. Jack finds a goblet. These are the robbers' treasure.

paragraphs.context: “Actually, I felt something, too,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack touches the cold thing again and feels its shape. It is a goblet.

background.note: A goblet is a cup with a stem and a base. Rich people in the Middle Ages drank from gold or silver goblets.

paragraphs.context: “I just found something else,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie finds something so heavy she cannot lift it with one hand.

paragraphs.context: When Jack tried to pick the object up, he almost dropped it.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels a head, a nose, wings and claws. They have found the dragon!

paragraphs.context: Jack stuffed the heavy object in his backpack.
paragraphs.simple: They crawl back out. The waterfall sprays them with water.

paragraphs.context: Jack set down his backpack and pulled out the object.
paragraphs.simple: In the moonlight the gold dragon is beautiful. Its wings are raised, and it seems to look at the far hills.

background.note: Gold does not rust or turn dark, so gold statues stay shiny for a very long time.

paragraphs.context: “Your Majesties!” Annie called. “We found the ninth dragon!”
paragraphs.simple: They run to the cart, but the king and queen are not there.

paragraphs.context: Guinevere was kneeling on the grass, holding Arthur in her arms.
paragraphs.simple: The queen holds the king. She says he is dying.

paragraphs.context: “He can’t be,” said Jack. Not now.
paragraphs.simple: Jack gets the flask, but there is no healing water left.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard a faint whinnying sound and the thunder of horse hooves.
paragraphs.simple: Riders are coming. The queen says they are the robbers, coming back for their treasure.

paragraphs.context: Jack started to tremble. The king was dying. The enemy was coming.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is scared. The queen says there is no hope, but Jack says there is.

paragraphs.context: “We just have to keep going,” said Jack. “We have to do the next right thing.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they must keep going and do the next right thing, but he does not know what it is.

paragraphs.context: “Wait a minute,” said Annie. “I just remembered! Our stones from Cafelle!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers Cafelle's red stones. They must use them with hope, strength and imagination.

paragraphs.context: Jack clasped his stone. He stared at the dragon statue and tried to feel hopeful and strong
paragraphs.simple: Jack holds his stone and shouts good wishes for the king and queen. Annie wishes for goodness and kindness.

background.note: "Long live the king!" is an old English cry. People shout it when a new king or queen begins to rule.

paragraphs.context: As Jack and Annie shouted their words, the gold dragon began to glow as if it were lit from within.
paragraphs.simple: The gold dragon gets brighter and hotter until it looks like it is on fire.

paragraphs.context: “Long live Camelot!” said Jack. “And Morgan’s library and all the books!”
paragraphs.simple: They shout for Camelot, the library, books, gardens, music, myths and legends.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard thunder, but it wasn’t the thunder of horse hooves.
paragraphs.simple: The noise and shaking come from the statue. Even the air around it is shaking.

paragraphs.context: Hissing, cracking, screaming sounds rocked the night.
paragraphs.simple: There is a huge explosion. A cloud bursts from the top of the mountain and catches fire, and a giant red dragon rises from the flames.

background.note: The red dragon is the symbol of Wales and is on the Welsh flag. In old Welsh stories, a red dragon fights a white dragon under a hill, and young Merlin explains it.

paragraphs.context: The dragon’s eyes were flaming. Its horns and claws and scaly skin flashed in the moonlight.
paragraphs.simple: The dragon's wings make a great wind, and a magic door opens. Jack sees pictures of magic lands and creatures fly past. Then everything is dark.

background.note: Some of these creatures come from earlier Merlin Missions, such as the Ice Wizard, the Raven King and the Sea Serpent.
In Scottish stories, a water horse (kelpie) is a magic horse that lives in lakes and rivers.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. He was sitting in soft wet grass,
paragraphs.simple: Jack wakes up on wet grass, still holding the red stone. Annie, the king and queen are near him.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard water splashing. It sounded as if fish were jumping,
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears splashing, but a golden mist over a lake hides everything. The air smells of flowers.

paragraphs.context: “We were pulled into the portal, and it brought us to Avalon,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the magic door brought them to Avalon. The queen agrees.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie turned around. Guinevere was sitting up,
paragraphs.simple: The queen looks confused but happy. Jack and Annie say they are fine.

paragraphs.context: Guinevere smiled at them. Then she reached out and tenderly touched the king’s shoulder.
paragraphs.simple: The queen gently wakes the king. Oki licks his face, and he laughs.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked down and saw the gold statue shining in the dewy grass.
paragraphs.simple: The gold statue is next to Jack and is still warm. Jack asks about the giant living dragon.

paragraphs.context: “And I,” said the king, sitting up. Arthur’s voice was hoarse, but his eyes were clear.
paragraphs.simple: The king saw the dragon too. His face has color again, and he says his wound is starting to heal.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly Oki let out a yelp. Then the puppy dashed to the shore of the lake and barked wildly.
paragraphs.simple: Beautiful singing comes across the lake. The king says it is mermaids.

background.note: Stories of mermaids are told all over the world. In Britain there are many old stories of mermaids singing to sailors.

paragraphs.context: Jack just smiled. In this strange new world, nothing seemed impossible.
paragraphs.simple: In this magic place, Jack believes everything can happen.

paragraphs.context: Slowly, a cinnamon-colored boat with a white sail glided out of the haze.
paragraphs.simple: A boat comes out of the mist. Merlin is steering it, and a small penguin stands next to him.

background.note: Jack and Annie met Penny in Antarctica in Magic Tree House #40, Eve of the Emperor Penguin, and brought her to Merlin.

paragraphs.context: When Merlin saw Jack and Annie, his eyes grew wide with astonishment.
paragraphs.simple: Merlin is very surprised and asks how they came to Avalon. Annie says "Magic!"

paragraphs.context: Merlin landed the small sailboat, and he and Penny came ashore.
paragraphs.simple: Oki and Penny meet and play together.

paragraphs.context: Merlin cried out in amazement when he saw the king and queen walking toward him.
paragraphs.simple: The king tells Merlin about the invaders.

paragraphs.context: As he began telling Merlin the story of the invaders, a snow-white unicorn pranced out of the golden haze.
paragraphs.simple: A white unicorn comes out of the mist with Teddy and Kathleen on its back.

background.note: Dianthus is the unicorn from Magic Tree House #36, Blizzard of the Blue Moon. Jack and Annie rescued him in New York City.

paragraphs.context: Teddy and Kathleen shouted with wonder and joy when they saw Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy and Kathleen jump down and hug Jack and Annie. Oki jumps around the unicorn.

paragraphs.context: “Why have you come here?” asked Kathleen.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells them the king was wounded but is better now. They hope Morgan can heal him.

paragraphs.context: Teddy peered into the mist. “She’s…there!” he said, pointing toward the water.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan comes out of the mist in a small boat pulled by swans.

paragraphs.context: Morgan looked bewildered to see them.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan is very surprised. Jack and Annie tell her everything.

background.note: In some versions of the legend, Morgan le Fay and other queens carry the wounded King Arthur to Avalon in a boat.

paragraphs.context: Morgan crossed to King Arthur. “Welcome back to the Isle of Avalon, Your Majesty,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan puts her hand on the king's chest. She says he will be healed, but he and the queen must stay in Avalon for a while.

background.note: Writers in the 1100s, such as Geoffrey of Monmouth, first wrote about Avalon as the island where Arthur's sword Excalibur was made.

paragraphs.context: “I fear they must return to Camelot,” said Merlin, stepping forward.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie must take the gold dragon back to the garden before the sun rises, or its power will be lost forever.

background.note: A full moon rises at about sunset and sets at about sunrise, so it shines all night.

paragraphs.context: “But the dragon is not in its place now,” said Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy asks how they can go back without the dragon. Morgan says they will go back the same way they came.

paragraphs.context: “Oh!” said Jack. He felt in his pocket for the piece of volcanic rock.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says the stones and their words of hope will call the dragon again.

paragraphs.context: “And I will tell her that you saved my life,” King Arthur said.
paragraphs.simple: The king and queen thank Jack and Annie. The king says he will return and rebuild the kingdom.

paragraphs.context: Everyone grew quiet. Annie and Jack took the red stones from their pockets.
paragraphs.simple: Holding the stones and the statue, Jack and Annie whisper "Long live Camelot" with all their hearts.

paragraphs.context: Grasping their stones, Jack and Annie whispered these words over and over with hope and strength,
paragraphs.simple: Wind and colored clouds come. The dragon appears in a red sky and carries them back to Camelot.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said Jack. In the first light of dawn, he could see the tangles of vines and flowers,
paragraphs.simple: In the early morning light, they are back in Morgan's secret garden.

paragraphs.context: Oki leapt from Annie’s arms and scurried among the patches of ivy, wild grasses, and shrubs,
paragraphs.simple: Oki runs around barking at the eight other dragon statues.

paragraphs.context: “The ninth dragon goes behind those yellow rosebushes,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the gold dragon back behind the yellow roses. They leave Cafelle's stones there too. The dragon shines in the morning sun.

paragraphs.context: “Let’s go,” said Jack. And the three of them left Morgan’s garden.
paragraphs.simple: They walk back through the library and passages to the outer courtyard.

background.note: Morgan's library is where Jack and Annie usually start their Merlin Missions.

paragraphs.context: Sir Lamorak and Sir Tristan were standing by the entrance gate.
paragraphs.simple: The two knights are guarding the gate. They turn around quickly in surprise.

paragraphs.context: “Where are the king and queen?” said Sir Tristan.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie say the king and queen are safe in Avalon and will come back when the king is well.

paragraphs.context: “And the king said to tell you that he’ll work with his knights and all his subjects to restore order to the kingdom,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack gives the king's message: he will work with his knights and his people to make the kingdom safe again.

background.note: People who live under a king or queen are called that ruler's subjects. People in Britain were called British subjects for a long time.

paragraphs.context: “Bye for now,” said Annie. “Hold down the fort!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie jokes with the knights: "Take care of the castle while we are away!"

background.note: "Hold down the fort" is an American saying from the 1800s. It first meant to defend a fort against attack.

paragraphs.context: Jack, Annie, and Oki headed out the castle entrance gate and started through the hay field.
paragraphs.simple: They run through the field and the forest. Oki leads them to the magic tree house.

background.note: Oaks can live for hundreds of years. In Britain, very old oaks are often linked with legends, such as the Major Oak of Robin Hood.

paragraphs.context: He lifted the puppy and put him into his pack.
paragraphs.simple: Annie points at a picture of Frog Creek and wishes to go there. The tree house spins.

background.note: The tree house always has a book about the place it goes. To go home, Jack and Annie point at a picture of Frog Creek in a book about Pennsylvania.

paragraphs.context: The day was cloudy and cool. No time had passed in the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.simple: They are home. No time has passed while they were away.

paragraphs.context: “Dog park? Are you serious?” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot believe Annie still wants to go to the dog park. She says she is not tired.

paragraphs.context: “Not really,” said Annie. “Oki just led us to the magic tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Annie lists everything they did: the seer, the robbers, the cart, the riddle, the cave, the dragon, Avalon, the unicorn and the mermaids. Then she says it was nothing much.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: she makes a huge adventure sound small.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded. “Okay. What you’re saying is Oki just took us on a little detour on our way to the dog park.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack jokes that the whole adventure was just a short side trip on the way to the dog park.

paragraphs.context: “Sure, why not?” said Jack as they headed out of the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to buy a toothbrush for Oki at the pet store. They both love their ordinary lives.

background.note: Vets say that brushing a dog's teeth with special dog toothpaste helps keep them healthy. Human toothpaste is not safe for dogs.
